note.explanation: Acids and bases can be described by the ions they produce in water or by proton transfer. Acids react with some metals, carbonates and bases in characteristic ways. Some substances, such as water and hydrogen carbonate ions, can act as either acids or bases.
note.checkAnswer: HSO₄⁻ donates H⁺ to form SO₄²⁻, so it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
note.simple: An acid can give away a proton, H⁺. A base can accept H⁺. In water, acids produce H₃O⁺ and bases produce OH⁻ or accept H⁺. Reactions help us identify acids and bases.
note.checkQuestion: How does HSO₄⁻ show that it is a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
note.title: Acids and Bases: Key Ideas
steps: Identify the acid and base using the definition named in the question.
For a reaction, write the correct products and balance the equation.
For proton transfer, show which species loses H⁺ and which gains H⁺.
For an acid–carbonate reaction, include salt, water and carbon dioxide.
note.answer: An acid donates H⁺; a base accepts H⁺. Acid–base reactions form products such as salts, water, carbon dioxide or hydrogen, depending on the reactants.

mcqs.stem: Q7.1. Which acid is not used as a food or mixed with food?
rationales: Tartaric acid is used in foods.
Ascorbic acid is vitamin C and is used in foods.
Citric acid is commonly used in foods.
Formic acid is not used as a food or mixed with food.

mcqs.stem: Q7.2. While baking, which gas is responsible for raising the bread and making it soft?
rationales: Oxygen does not produce the raising effect described.
Carbon dioxide bubbles raise the dough and make bread soft.
Nitrogen is not the gas responsible for raising bread.
Carbon monoxide is not responsible for raising bread.

options: All the above mentioned characteristics are true
mcqs.stem: Q7.3. Predict the main characteristics of the reactions of metals with acids.
rationales: The metal is consumed as it reacts with the acid.
The metal forms a salt with the acid’s anion.
Hydrogen gas is commonly evolved when a metal reacts with an acid.
All three statements describe the reaction.

mcqs.stem: Q7.4. How many hydroxide ions, calcium hydroxide will release in water?
rationales: Each formula unit of Ca(OH)₂ contains two OH⁻ ions, not one.
Ca(OH)₂ releases two hydroxide ions per formula unit.
Calcium hydroxide does release hydroxide ions in water.
It contains two hydroxide ions, not three.

mcqs.stem: Q7.5. In a neutralization reaction between KOH and H₃PO₄, how many molecules of KOH will react with one molecule of H₃PO₄?
rationales: Two KOH molecules would not neutralize all three acidic hydrogens.
One KOH molecule neutralizes only one acidic hydrogen.
Three KOH molecules neutralize the three acidic hydrogens in H₃PO₄.
Four KOH molecules are more than needed for complete neutralization.

mcqs.stem: Q7.6. Which acid is used in the preparation of soap?
rationales: Tartaric acid is not the acid used to prepare soap.
Citric acid is not the acid used to prepare soap.
Stearic acid is a fatty acid used in soap preparation.
Oxalic acid is not the acid used to prepare soap.

mcqs.stem: Q7.7. Which compound is formed when SO₂ is dissolved in water?
rationales: SO₃ is not the product of dissolving SO₂ in water.
SO₂ + H₂O forms H₂SO₃.
H₂SO₄ is not formed simply by dissolving SO₂ in water.
H₂S₂O₇ is not the product of this reaction.

mcqs.stem: Q7.8. Which of the following contains oxalic acid?
rationales: Tomato contains oxalic acid.
Orange is associated with citric acid, not the requested answer.
Tamarind is associated with tartaric acid.
Sour milk contains lactic acid.

mcqs.stem:
Q7.9. Which compound in the following reaction is behaving as a conjugate base?

CH₃COOH (aq) + H₂O (l) → CH₃COO⁻ (aq) + H₃O⁺ (aq)
rationales: CH₃COOH donates a proton and acts as the acid.
H₂O accepts a proton and acts as the base.
CH₃COO⁻ is formed when CH₃COOH loses H⁺, so it is the conjugate base.
H₃O⁺ is formed when water accepts H⁺, so it is the conjugate acid.

options: Reaction of an acid with a metal carbonate
Reaction of an acid with metal hydrogen carbonate
Reaction of an alkali with an acid
Reaction of an alkali with ammonium salt
mcqs.stem: Q7.10. When a chemical reaction is carried out with a substance Z; a gas is produced which turns red litmus paper blue. What is the reaction?
rationales: An acid–carbonate reaction produces CO₂, which does not turn red litmus blue.
An acid–hydrogen carbonate reaction also produces CO₂, not a basic gas.
Neutralization between an alkali and an acid does not produce a gas that turns red litmus blue.
An alkali reacting with an ammonium salt can produce ammonia, which turns moist red litmus blue.

written.text:
Choose Arrhenius Acids among the following compounds.
HF, NH₄⁺, H₂SO₃, SO₃, H₂S, H₂O
written.finalAnswer: HF, NH₄⁺, H₂SO₃ and H₂S

rubric.why: Identify the molecular acids that increase hydrogen-ion concentration in water.
rubric.description: Names HF, H₂SO₃ and H₂S.
rubric.how: Select the three compounds that act as acids in aqueous solution.

rubric.why: The ammonium ion can produce hydronium ions by transferring a proton to water.
rubric.description: Includes NH₄⁺ as acidic in water.
rubric.how: Recognize that NH₄⁺ can donate H⁺ to water.

rubric.why: SO₃ is an acidic oxide, not an Arrhenius acid itself, and water is not selected here.
rubric.description: Does not select SO₃ or H₂O.
rubric.how: Exclude the oxide and water from the list.

modelAnswer: HF, NH₄⁺, H₂SO₃ and H₂S produce H⁺ (or H₃O⁺) in water.
SO₃ is an acidic oxide, while H₂O is not selected as an Arrhenius acid here.

written.text: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?
written.finalAnswer: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂

rubric.why: The products show the salt and hydrogen gas formed.
rubric.description: Gives CaSO₄ and H₂ as products.
rubric.how: Use calcium’s sulfate salt and hydrogen gas as the products.

rubric.why: A correct balanced equation communicates the reaction clearly.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced reaction equation.
rubric.how: Write Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂.

modelAnswer: Ca + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂
Calcium sulfate forms as a coating, so it can slow further reaction.

written.text: Which salt is formed when HCl reacts with BaCO₃?
written.finalAnswer: BaCl₂ (barium chloride)

rubric.why: Identifies the salt produced from barium and chloride ions.
rubric.description: Names barium chloride.
rubric.how: Combine Ba²⁺ with Cl⁻ to form BaCl₂.

rubric.why: The complete reaction confirms the salt is correctly identified.
rubric.description: Gives the balanced carbonate reaction.
rubric.how: Write BaCO₃ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O.

modelAnswer: BaCO₃ + 2HCl → BaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O
The salt formed is barium chloride, BaCl₂.

written.text: How will you justify that HSO₄⁻ is a Brønsted – Lowry acid?
written.finalAnswer: HSO₄⁻ donates H⁺ to form SO₄²⁻.

rubric.why: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor.
rubric.description: States that HSO₄⁻ donates a proton.
rubric.how: Identify the proton transfer from HSO₄⁻.

rubric.why: The conjugate base formed verifies the proton loss.
rubric.description: Shows formation of SO₄²⁻.
rubric.how: Write HSO₄⁻ → H⁺ + SO₄²⁻.

modelAnswer: HSO₄⁻ → H⁺ + SO₄²⁻
HSO₄⁻ donates a proton, so it is a Brønsted–Lowry acid.

written.text: Why is HCl not edible although it is present in the stomach and responsible for digestion of food?
written.finalAnswer: HCl is a corrosive strong acid; stomach lining protects the body from it.

rubric.why: Recognizes the harmful, corrosive nature of hydrochloric acid outside the protected stomach.
rubric.description: States that HCl is corrosive or a strong acid.
rubric.how: Explain that HCl is not safe to eat as a substance.

rubric.why: Explains why its normal presence in the stomach does not make it edible.
rubric.description: Mentions the stomach’s protective lining or mucus.
rubric.how: State that the stomach wall is protected from its acid.

modelAnswer: HCl is a strong, corrosive acid and is not safe to eat.
The stomach lining and its protective mucus help protect the stomach from its own HCl.

written.text: What chemical name will you give to soap as a compound?
written.finalAnswer: Sodium or potassium salts of higher fatty acids

rubric.why: Soap is chemically a salt of a fatty acid.
rubric.description: Identifies soap as a salt of fatty acids.
rubric.how: Use the chemical class name rather than treating soap as one pure molecule.

rubric.why: Common soaps contain sodium or potassium as the counter-ion.
rubric.description: Names sodium or potassium salts.
rubric.how: State that soap is a sodium or potassium salt of a higher fatty acid.

modelAnswer: Soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a higher fatty acid.

written.text:
In the presence of a drop of an acid, water is known to ionize as follows:

H₂O (l) ⇌ H⁺ (aq) + OH⁻ (aq)

In your opinion, which name will be suitable for water: an acid, a base or both?
written.finalAnswer: Both: water can act as an acid or a base.

rubric.why: Water can participate in proton transfer in either direction.
rubric.description: Identifies water as both an acid and a base.
rubric.how: Choose both rather than only acid or only base.

rubric.why: The explanation links water’s behaviour to proton loss and gain.
rubric.description: Explains its ability to donate or accept a proton.
rubric.how: State that water can donate H⁺ to form OH⁻ or accept H⁺ to form H₃O⁺.

modelAnswer: Water can act as both an acid and a base.
It can donate H⁺ to form OH⁻ or accept H⁺ to form H₃O⁺.

written.text: Why does Na₂CO₃ behave like a base in water?
written.finalAnswer: CO₃²⁻ accepts H⁺ from water and forms OH⁻ ions.

rubric.why: Carbonate-ion proton acceptance explains the basic behaviour.
rubric.description: States that CO₃²⁻ accepts a proton from water.
rubric.how: Show the proton-accepting action of carbonate.

rubric.why: Hydroxide ions account for the basic solution.
rubric.description: States that OH⁻ ions are produced.
rubric.how: Include hydroxide formation in the explanation.

modelAnswer: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻
The OH⁻ ions make the solution basic.

written.text: Is NaHCO₃ a base or an acid? Justify your answer.
written.finalAnswer: NaHCO₃ can act as both an acid and a base; HCO₃⁻ can donate or accept H⁺.

rubric.why: Hydrogen carbonate is able to take either role in proton transfer.
rubric.description: Identifies NaHCO₃/HCO₃⁻ as able to act as both.
rubric.how: Answer that it can behave as an acid and a base.

rubric.why: The proton-transfer examples justify the classification.
rubric.description: Explains the two proton-transfer possibilities.
rubric.how: State that HCO₃⁻ can lose H⁺ to form CO₃²⁻ or gain H⁺ to form H₂CO₃.

modelAnswer: NaHCO₃ can act as both an acid and a base.
HCO₃⁻ can donate H⁺ to form CO₃²⁻ or accept H⁺ to form H₂CO₃.

written.text: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
written.finalAnswer: A strong acid ionizes completely; a concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid per volume of solution.

rubric.why: Strength describes how completely acid particles ionize in water.
rubric.description: Defines a strong acid by complete or nearly complete ionization.
rubric.how: Explain the extent of ionization.

rubric.why: Concentration describes the amount of solute in a given solution volume.
rubric.description: Defines a concentrated acid by its amount per volume.
rubric.how: Explain that concentration is about how much acid is present in the solution.

modelAnswer: A strong acid ionizes completely or almost completely in water.
A concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid in a given volume of solution.

written.text: Explain Arrhenius concept of acids and bases.
written.finalAnswer: An Arrhenius acid produces H⁺ ions in water; an Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ ions in water.

rubric.why: This is the defining Arrhenius behaviour of an acid.
rubric.description: Defines an Arrhenius acid.
rubric.how: State that an acid increases H⁺ (or H₃O⁺) in aqueous solution.

rubric.why: This is the defining Arrhenius behaviour of a base.
rubric.description: Defines an Arrhenius base.
rubric.how: State that a base produces OH⁻ in water.

rubric.why: The Arrhenius definitions specifically refer to aqueous solution.
rubric.description: Specifies the aqueous condition.
rubric.how: Make clear that the ions are produced in water.

modelAnswer: According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
A base produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.

written.text: Compare Arrhenius and Brønsted – Lowry concepts of acids and bases.
written.finalAnswer: Arrhenius: acids produce H⁺ in water and bases produce OH⁻ in water. Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate H⁺ and bases accept H⁺.

rubric.why: The acid definition is a key part of the Arrhenius concept.
rubric.description: Gives the Arrhenius acid definition.
rubric.how: State that an Arrhenius acid produces H⁺ in water.

rubric.why: The base definition completes the Arrhenius comparison.
rubric.description: Gives the Arrhenius base definition.
rubric.how: State that an Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ in water.

rubric.why: The Brønsted–Lowry acid definition is based on proton transfer.
rubric.description: Defines a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
rubric.how: State that it donates a proton.

rubric.why: The Brønsted–Lowry base definition completes the comparison.
rubric.description: Defines a Brønsted–Lowry base.
rubric.how: State that it accepts a proton.

modelAnswer: Arrhenius: an acid produces H⁺ in water, while a base produces OH⁻ in water.
Brønsted–Lowry: an acid donates a proton (H⁺), while a base accepts a proton (H⁺).
The Brønsted–Lowry concept describes proton transfer and is not restricted to aqueous solution.

written.text: How does sulphuric acid react with NH₄Cl?
written.finalAnswer: NH₄Cl + H₂SO₄ → NH₄HSO₄ + HCl

rubric.why: Identifies the products of the acid reaction.
rubric.description: Gives ammonium hydrogen sulfate and hydrogen chloride.
rubric.how: Write both products correctly.

rubric.why: The equation shows the reactants and balanced stoichiometry.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation.
rubric.how: Write NH₄Cl + H₂SO₄ → NH₄HSO₄ + HCl.

modelAnswer: NH₄Cl + H₂SO₄ → NH₄HSO₄ + HCl

written.text: How does sulphuric acid react with NH₄NO₃?
written.finalAnswer: NH₄NO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NH₄HSO₄ + HNO₃

rubric.why: Identifies the products formed in the reaction.
rubric.description: Gives ammonium hydrogen sulfate and nitric acid.
rubric.how: Write both products correctly.

rubric.why: A correct equation shows the reaction and balanced atoms.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation.
rubric.how: Write NH₄NO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NH₄HSO₄ + HNO₃.

modelAnswer: NH₄NO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NH₄HSO₄ + HNO₃

written.text: How does sulphuric acid react with MgO?
written.finalAnswer: MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O

rubric.why: An acid reacting with a basic oxide forms salt and water.
rubric.description: Gives magnesium sulfate and water.
rubric.how: Identify the salt and water products.

rubric.why: A balanced equation demonstrates the reaction accurately.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation.
rubric.how: Write MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O.

modelAnswer: MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O

written.text: How does sulphuric acid react with MgCO₃?
written.finalAnswer: MgCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O

rubric.why: Acid–carbonate reactions form a salt, carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.description: Names all three products.
rubric.how: Include MgSO₄, CO₂ and H₂O.

rubric.why: The balanced equation shows the reaction correctly.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation.
rubric.how: Write MgCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O.

modelAnswer: MgCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O

written.text: What happens when a base reacts with a non-metallic oxide. What do you infer about the nature of non-metallic oxide?
written.finalAnswer: A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form salt and water; the oxide is acidic.

rubric.why: The salt is a principal product of the reaction.
rubric.description: States that a salt forms.
rubric.how: Describe the reaction product.

rubric.why: Water is the other expected product in the general reaction.
rubric.description: States that water forms.
rubric.how: Include water as a product.

rubric.why: Reaction with a base supports classifying the non-metallic oxide as acidic.
rubric.description: Infers that the non-metallic oxide is acidic in nature.
rubric.how: State that non-metallic oxides are acidic oxides.

modelAnswer: A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form salt and water.
Therefore, a non-metallic oxide has acidic nature.

written.text: State the reason of showing acidic character by both dry HCl gas and HCl solution in water.
written.finalAnswer: HCl shows acidic character because it donates H⁺; in water it forms H₃O⁺, and in the gaseous state it can donate a proton to a base.

rubric.why: Proton donation explains acidic character in the Brønsted–Lowry concept.
rubric.description: Identifies HCl as a proton donor.
rubric.how: State that HCl donates H⁺.

rubric.why: Hydronium formation explains the acid behaviour of its aqueous solution.
rubric.description: Explains that HCl in water forms H₃O⁺.
rubric.how: Include HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.

rubric.why: Proton transfer to a base can occur without water, for example with ammonia.
rubric.description: Explains proton transfer by gaseous HCl to a base.
rubric.how: Mention a base as the proton acceptor in the gas phase.

rubric.why: The proton-transfer idea links the two cases.
rubric.description: Connects both cases to proton donation.
rubric.how: Name proton transfer or the Brønsted–Lowry concept.

modelAnswer: HCl is acidic because it can donate a proton (H⁺) to a base.
In water, HCl forms H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.
Dry HCl gas can also donate H⁺ to a base such as NH₃, forming NH₄⁺.
Thus, its acidic character is due to proton donation.

written.text: Differentiate between an acid and its conjugate base.
written.finalAnswer: An acid donates H⁺; its conjugate base is the species left after the acid loses H⁺ and can accept H⁺.

rubric.why: Defines the acid by its proton-transfer role.
rubric.description: States that an acid donates H⁺.
rubric.how: Give the proton-donor definition.

rubric.why: Shows how the conjugate base is related to its acid.
rubric.description: States that it remains after the acid loses H⁺.
rubric.how: Explain the one-proton difference.

rubric.why: Describes the conjugate base’s ability to regain the proton.
rubric.description: States that the conjugate base can accept H⁺.
rubric.how: Give its proton-acceptor role.

rubric.why: A conjugate pair example makes the distinction clear.
rubric.description: Gives a valid conjugate acid–base pair.
rubric.how: For example, CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻.

modelAnswer: An acid donates H⁺ to another species.
The conjugate base is formed when the acid loses H⁺.
The conjugate base can accept H⁺ again.
For example, CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻ are a conjugate acid–base pair.

written.text: Acids play significant roles within human body. Comment on this statement.
written.finalAnswer: Acids are important in digestion, body chemistry and normal cell functions, but their amount and location must be controlled.

rubric.why: Stomach hydrochloric acid is an important example of an acid’s role.
rubric.description: Explains the role of HCl in digestion.
rubric.how: Mention stomach acid and its part in digestion.

rubric.why: Acidity and pH affect the action of enzymes and body reactions.
rubric.description: Connects pH to enzymes or body chemistry.
rubric.how: Explain that suitable pH is needed for enzyme function.

rubric.why: Acids and related molecules are important in body structures and processes.
rubric.description: Gives another relevant acid-related role or molecule.
rubric.how: Mention amino acids, proteins, fatty acids or another valid example.

rubric.why: The body needs to keep acidity within safe limits.
rubric.description: Mentions control of acidity or pH.
rubric.how: State that body pH must be regulated.

rubric.why: A clear conclusion directly comments on the statement.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant concluding comment.
rubric.how: Conclude that acids have important functions in the body.

modelAnswer: Acids have important roles in the human body.
Hydrochloric acid in the stomach helps digestion and provides an acidic environment.
A suitable pH is also needed for enzymes and other body reactions to work properly.
Amino acids are building blocks of proteins, and fatty acids are important in the body.
The amount and location of acids must be controlled so that body functions remain normal.

written.text: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water for a short duration?
written.finalAnswer: Lime water turns milky because insoluble CaCO₃ forms.

rubric.why: The visible observation is the expected evidence of the reaction.
rubric.description: States that lime water turns milky or gives a white precipitate.
rubric.how: Describe the observed change.

rubric.why: Calcium carbonate explains the milky appearance.
rubric.description: Identifies the precipitate as CaCO₃.
rubric.how: Write CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O.

modelAnswer: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O
Insoluble CaCO₃ forms, so the lime water turns milky.

written.text: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water for a long duration?
written.finalAnswer: The milkiness disappears because soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate forms.

rubric.why: Excess carbon dioxide removes the initial suspended precipitate.
rubric.description: States that the milkiness disappears or the solution clears.
rubric.how: Describe the observation after passing CO₂ for a long time.

rubric.why: The soluble product accounts for the clearing of the solution.
rubric.description: Names soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate.
rubric.how: Write CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂.

modelAnswer: CaCO₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → Ca(HCO₃)₂
Soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate forms, so the milkiness disappears.

examTips: Section A tests key facts, formulas, ion counts and identification of reaction products; learn the characteristic products and balance equations.
Short answers commonly ask for a salt, a definition-based classification or a reaction equation. Give the key reason as well as the answer.
For descriptive reactions, show reactants, products and a balanced equation. For acid–carbonate reactions, remember salt + CO₂ + water.
Comparison questions earn marks when both sides are defined separately and the difference is stated clearly.
Investigative questions ask for observations and the chemical reason behind them; give both, such as the change in lime water and the precipitate responsible.

hints: Recall the products formed when an acid reacts with a carbonate.
Write the magnesium salt, carbon dioxide and water, then check that the equation is balanced.
yourTurn.question: How does sulphuric acid react with MgCO₃?
solution: The salt, carbon dioxide and water are formed.

hints: Think about the initial precipitate formed when CO₂ enters lime water.
With excess CO₂, that precipitate reacts further to make a soluble product.
yourTurn.question: What is observed when CO₂ is passed through lime water for a long duration?
solution: The initial CaCO₃ precipitate reacts with excess CO₂ and water.
The soluble product makes the milkiness disappear.
yourTurn.answer: The milkiness disappears because soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate forms.

steps.why: Calcium is a metal and sulfuric acid supplies the sulfate ion; metals reacting with acids form a salt and hydrogen.
steps.text: Question: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?

steps.why: This is the reaction pattern for a metal with an acid: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
steps.text: Given: calcium metal, Ca; dilute sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄.

steps.why: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ and sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so their salt formula is CaSO₄.
steps.text: Products: calcium sulfate, CaSO₄, and hydrogen gas, H₂.

steps.why: One atom of each element is balanced on both sides, including two hydrogen atoms as H₂.
The equation gives the products and the balanced chemical result.

example.question: How does calcium metal react with dilute H₂SO₄?

explain.title: Two ways to define acids and bases
explain.body: In the Arrhenius concept, an acid produces H⁺ in water and a base produces OH⁻ in water. In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺.

explain.title: Acids react in familiar patterns
explain.body: A metal reacting with an acid commonly forms a salt and hydrogen. An acid reacting with a carbonate forms a salt, carbon dioxide and water. An acid reacting with a base or basic oxide forms a salt and water.

explain.title: Acid strength is not concentration
explain.body: Strength describes the extent to which an acid ionizes in water. Concentration describes how much acid is present in a given volume of solution.

explain.title: Conjugate acid–base pairs differ by H⁺
explain.body: When an acid donates H⁺, the species left is its conjugate base. For example, CH₃COOH donates H⁺ to form CH₃COO⁻.

explain.title: Some oxides and ions can act both ways
explain.body: Non-metallic oxides generally show acidic character by reacting with bases. Water and HCO₃⁻ can take part in proton transfer as either an acid or a base.

mistakes: Do not confuse acid strength with acid concentration; one describes ionization and the other amount per volume.
Do not forget that acid–carbonate reactions produce carbon dioxide as well as salt and water.
Balance equations and write correct ion charges in formulas, such as CaSO₄ and BaCl₂.
A conjugate base is formed after an acid loses H⁺; it is not the species formed after gaining H⁺.
For the lime-water test, distinguish the short-duration milky precipitate from the clearing caused by excess CO₂.
Do not claim that every acidic substance must contain an ionised hydrogen already; explain proton transfer or ion formation in water as appropriate.
